subject: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates

messages.author: 41efe665757ab054
messages.subject: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
parts:
Hi Lavaan Users and Developers!

I'm a developer on the OpenMx SEM project.  One of the things I've been working lately is weighted least squares (WLS).  I've noticed an odd behavior for WLS when there are both ordinal (categorical) and continuous variables.  In this case, using the full WLS produces positively biased estimates, but the estimates from diagonally WLS or ULS are fine.  When I first observed this in OpenMx, I thought it was a bug in my code, but then I replicated the same behavior in lavaan.  I've attached an R script that demonstrates the behavior in OpenMx and lavaan, and a screen grab that shows the final result from line 248 for that script.

The question to me is "why does this happen?".  Is this a known issue with WLS, and if so then are there any citations that discuss this?  So far I haven't been able to find anything about it.  Thanks for your help!

-Mike Hunter

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
parts:
Mike--
     Don't have a cite, but this reminds me of a problem with mixed continuous and ordinal variables with the LISREL package.  Some years back (how they pass), someone pointed out that matrices of mixed continuous and ordinal variables could produce some bizarre polyserial correlations--to the point where someone might be advised to try treating a few ordinal variables as if they were continuous.  The results were less bad than facing this problem with mixed variable types.  I don't know if this issue was ever resolved, or if lavaan's approach has anything in common with this polychoric / polyserial problem.  Also, full-blown WLS is very demanding in terms of sample size, and can be decidedly unstable at sample sizes less than multiple thousands.  That is part of why diagonally weighted least squares became so attractive as an alternative.  Some literature migth have emerged from this--but I'm not sure.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 41efe665757ab054
messages.subject: Re: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
parts:
Thanks for the reply, Ed!

Two small points may merit some clarification.  First, the polyserial correlations used are identical across WLS, DWLS, and ULS: only the weight matrices differ.  Second, the issue seems robust to sample size.  The original example had N=1,000.  I re-ran it with N=10,000 and N=20,000: the bias was unchanged.

The Muthén articles on three-stage WLS only ever argue for DWLS based on the computational intensity for getting the full weight matrix, never bias that it could produce.    

As of now, this is still a mystery to me.

-Mike Hunter


Muthén, B. O.
A General Structural Equation Model with Dichotomous Ordered Categorical, and Continuous Latent Variable Indicators
Psychometrika, 1984, 49, 115-132

Muthén, B.; du Toit, S. & Spisic, D.
Robust inference using weighted least squares and quadratic estimating equations in latent variable modeling with categorical and continuous outcomes
Unpublished Technical Report, 1997

parts:
Mike--
     OK, so it's not sample size and it's not the polyserial correlations themselves.  That leaves (pretty much) the weights assigned to the elements of the correlation matrix.  It would not surprise me to find that these are either incorrect or only correct for specific distributions of the observed variables.  That's a Yves question, and he's enjoying a break. These asymptotic weights, for polyserial correlations, have been a real nuisance to many people in this field.
     (Actually, I had understood--I believe from Linda M.--that Mplus no longer explicitly computed these intermediate correlations. It might be worthwhile to check with the Mplus folks and ask this specific question--do they compute polyserials or do they use an approach taht allows them to bypass this step?) 
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: b8fd92e5e3662745
messages.subject: Re: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
parts:
If the discrepancy does not go to zero with larger sample sizes, it
means that the model is misspecified. This is the foundation of
econometrics' Hausman test. ULS and DWLS only make assumptions
regarding the second order moments of the data, which you provide via
polychoric/polyserial correlations (and these may be misspecified in
their own right if the underlying data are not multivariate normal,
although you did simulate them as normal, so that should not be the
issue). In a continuous case with Pearson moment correlation not
having any of the weird problems, you can say that they estimate
parameters $\theta$ in $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}(\theta)$ with only the
model structure being used to drive the estimates. Full WLS/ADF tries
to bring some assumptions about the fourth order moments of the data
(warranted if these assumptions are reasonably close to be true) via
correlations of $\sigma_{ij}$. The second moment of second moments are
obviously the fourth moments. If these assumptions are not warranted,
the estimates get fragile. The full WLS/ADF estimates are dealing with
$\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}(\theta)$ AND fourth order moment = function
of $\theta$, which has a different solution in population (unless you
have the fourth order moments matching those of the multivariate
normal, or probably the more general Satorra's asymptotic robustness
conditions), so the WLS estimates must be converging to that different
target.

Economists utilize Hausman tests to check whether their model
assumptions are satisfied by fitting a model with a robust method
(DWLS) and a method that is efficient when the model is perfect
(WLS/ADF/normal theory MLE). When the model assumptions are satisfied,
the difference is only due to the lesser efficiency of the former
method, so the difference between the estimates should be within
sampling variation. In case of WLS/ADF vs DWLS and ULS, though, it
seems to be hard to tell if the resulting difference between estimate
is a test on model *structure* (which is what most practitioners would
be interested in), or rather a test on *distribution* (non-normality
of the population) which is an inalienable assumption of the
WLS/ADF/NTMLE; it may well be the latter.

That you reproduced the problem in different packages is great, but I
would still hope to see less of a discrepancy between them. Otherwise,
the world of SEM cannot talk about DWLS as a *method*, only as a black
box churning the numbers. The Mx black box may be 2" x 5" x 3", and
lavaan's black box may be 3" x 7" x 1", and Mplus may be 4" x 3" x
undisclosed (you need to pay the license charge to figure out what
that last dimension is), and if all these black boxes produce
different numbers, I personally don't see any reason to trust any of
these numbers until I see an explanation put forth by a developer as
to why these numbers would differ.

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)
-- Principal Survey Scientist, Abt SRBI
-- Education Officer, Survey Research Methods Section of the American
Statistical Association
-- Opinions stated in this email are mine only, and do not reflect the
position of my employer
-- http://stas.kolenikov.name

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
parts:
On 08/17/2015 08:25 PM, Michael Hunter wrote:
> Hi Lavaan Users and Developers!
>
> I'm a developer on the OpenMx SEM project. One of the things I've been
> working lately is weighted least squares (WLS). I've noticed an odd
> behavior for WLS when there are both ordinal (categorical) and
> continuous variables. In this case, using the full WLS produces
> positively biased estimates, but the estimates from diagonally WLS or
> ULS are fine.

Hello Michael.

Four months later, I (re)discover this interesting post. (In August, I
saw your post, thought it was interesting, and then -in true vacation
modus- forgot all about it.)

There is indeed bias when using WLS for your model/data combination, but
I think this is not due to a 'bug' in the software (or the methodology).
Reassuringly, Mplus gives exactly the same results as lavaan. For the
skeptics, I attach the dataset (mplus.raw, N=10000), and the mplus
input/output files, as well as the the lavaan output in lavaan_output.txt).

(As to why the numbers between OpenMx and lavaan are slightly different,
this is mostly a matter of how exactly the weight matrix is computed.
Different approaches are possible, and lavaan and OpenMx use slightly
different strategies. I do not think this matters much.)

As was correctly pointed out by Stas, the reason for the 'bias' in this
case is model misspecification! WLS is much less forgiving if the model
is misspecified, compared to DWLS/ULS and even ML. When the model is
closer to the data, the bias goes away. For example:

library(lavaan)
pop.model <- 'f =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 + 0.7*y3 + 0.5*y4 + 0.5*y5 + 0.5*y6'
Data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 10000L, standardized = TRUE)
fit <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = Data, estimator =
"WLS")
summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)
lavaan (0.5-20) converged normally after 16 iterations

Estimator WLS
Minimum Function Test Statistic 5.453
Degrees of freedom 9
P-value (Chi-square) 0.793

Parameter Estimates:

Standard Errors Standard

Estimate Std.Err Z-value P(>|z|) Std.lv Std.all

y1 1.000 0.704 0.700

y3 0.987 0.017 57.738 0.000 0.695 0.702

y5 0.688 0.016 41.815 0.000 0.484 0.486

Note also that this 'bias' has nothing to do with the
categorical/continuous combination. If we only use continuous data, we
observe the same bias. Using your data generation script:

cDat <- rmvnorm(10000, sigma=sigma)
jdat2 <- data.frame(cDat, scale(cDat+rnorm(prod(dim(cDat)))))
names(jdat2) <- c("y1","y2","y3","y4","y5","y6")

fit <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = jdat2, estimator =
"WLS", meanstructure = TRUE)

> summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)

while plain ML gives

> fitb <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = jdat2,
estimator = "ML", meanstructure = TRUE)
> summary(fitb, standardized = TRUE)

The 'upward' bias we observe in the factor loadings is largely due to a
'downward' bias in the estimation of the residual variances of the
(continuous) y-indicators. 2nd order estimators (closed-form marginal
ML, DWLS, ULS) can happily ignore the fourth-order moments, and adjust
these residual variances freely to optimize fit. The WLS method does not
have this luxury, and must obey the fourth-moment patterns as found in
the data.

I do agree there is not much literature discussing this, at least not in
the SEM context.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
parts:
Thanks, Yves!

Your point about the 'bias' being due to the misspecification of the factor model is well-taken.  When Stas said it I thought it had something to due with WLS being intrinsically misspecified because of how it approximates fourth-order moments for ordinal data.  Showing the same effect when there are only continuous data helped clarify that for me.  Thanks again for your efforts and insights on this!

-Mike Hunter

pop.model <- 'f =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 + 0.7*y3 + 0.5*y4 + 0.5*y5 + 0.5*y6'
Data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 10000L, standardized = TRUE)
fit <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = Data, estimator = "WLS")
summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)

The 'upward' bias we observe in the factor loadings is largely due to a 'downward' bias in the estimation of the residual variances of the (continuous) y-indicators. 2nd order estimators (closed-form marginal ML, DWLS, ULS) can happily ignore the fourth-order moments, and adjust these residual variances freely to optimize fit. The WLS method does not have this luxury, and must obey the fourth-moment patterns as found in the data.

I do agree there is not much literature discussing this, at least not in the SEM context.

Yves.
